analysis.one_liner: Requires Congress to pass a law before any major federal regulation can take effect.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote: referred to committee in June 1999, it sat in a House subcommittee until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under this bill, federal agencies could no longer issue binding rules on their own. Every major regulation would first have to be passed, word for word, as a bill by both the House and Senate and signed by the President before it could take effect. Congress writes a few hundred laws a session but agencies issue thousands of rules covering air quality, workplace safety, food safety, and consumer finance; the bill gave special fast-track procedures so a rule's opponents could force a vote, but nothing forced Congress to ever act. A rule Congress never voted on would simply never exist.
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses and industries that oppose federal regulation would gain the most: any new rule could be stopped by defeating it on a floor vote, or more simply, by never getting a vote at all. Members of Congress would also gain power over executive agencies, which is the accountability argument the bill's sponsor made. Ordinary citizens who believe unelected officials make too much law would get a mechanism to force Congress to own every rule.

how_it_helps.text: No major regulation could take effect until Congress enacted a bill consisting solely of that regulation's text, signed by the President.
Agencies would have to submit every proposed rule to both chambers with an explanation, and the majority leader of each chamber would have to introduce it as a bill within three legislative days.
The bill gave each rule a fast track: no committee referral, points of order waived, one hour of debate, amendments barred, and a mandatory vote within 60 calendar days if a member moved to proceed.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people who depend on federal rules for clean air and water, safe workplaces, safe food and drugs, and honest financial markets would bear the cost. Congress passed roughly 200-300 public laws in a typical session of this era while agencies finalized thousands of rules; most rules could never clear a two-chamber vote, so protections would lapse whenever Congress declined to act — a decision industry lobbying can influence heavily.
analysis.who_pays_short: Everyone relying on federal health and safety rules

drawbacks.text: The bill applied to every regulation of general applicability, excluding only narrow categories like interpretive rules and agency procedures; with thousands of such rules issued per Congress, most could never receive a floor vote and would die by default.

Supporters' core argument was that Article I gives legislative power only to Congress, and that rules written by unelected officials should not bind the public until elected lawmakers vote to enact them.

The honest cost of the design: it converted every protection into something Congress must affirmatively renew, in a chamber where concentrated industry lobbying is strongest, so environmental, workplace, and consumer rules would be far easier to stop than to pass.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The accountability idea — Congress should own the laws it lets agencies write — has real democratic appeal, and the bill's fast-track procedures were carefully built to give rules a fair path to a vote. But the arithmetic defeats the purpose: Congress cannot hold votes on thousands of rules, so the practical effect is that most regulation would end not by debate but by inaction, with the loudest opponents guaranteed a hearing and ordinary beneficiaries of rules guaranteed nothing. The design functions as a veto for regulated industries more than as accountability.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Judiciary Committee and its Commercial and Administrative Law Subcommittee in June 1999 and never came out; no committee, subcommittee, or floor vote was ever held before the Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Rep. J.D. Hayworth introduced the bill on June 22, 1999, joined by 55 cosponsors.
The Speaker sent it to both the Judiciary and Rules Committees; it was then referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Commercial and Administrative Law on June 28, 1999.
No further action of any kind appears in the record — no hearings, markups, committee vote, or floor action — and the bill expired when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal agencies and the existing regulatory system came out ahead: rules kept taking effect without a congressional vote, and regulated industries did not get the ability to kill any rule by stalling Congress. Ordinary people kept the protections that would have been put up for a vote one by one.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Agencies and the regulatory status quo

for.name: Rep. J.D. Hayworth
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and recruited 54 colleagues to cosponsor it.

against.name: Henry Hyde
against.what_they_did: The bill sat in his committee's Commercial and Administrative Law Subcommittee from June 1999 onward; he never brought it to a markup or committee vote.

against.name: House Rules Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill under a dual referral for provisions within its jurisdiction and took no recorded action.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and 53 of the 55 cosponsors were Republicans; only 2 Democrats signed on, and no action ever reached a recorded vote.

industries.industry: Regulated industries (manufacturing, energy, chemical, and financial firms)
industries.note: The bill would have let any federal rule be stopped by a House or Senate that declined to pass it, giving regulated businesses a practical veto over new health, safety, and environmental requirements. The public cost of that veto falls on people those rules protect.

Agencies would lose their core lawmaking function: nothing they issued could bind anyone until Congress enacted the text as a bill. This is the transfer of power the bill's sponsor was openly aiming at.
